title: Users and Permissions
oneLiner: Who can read, change and run each file, and how to change that with chmod and chgrp.
keyTakeaway: Every file has an owner, a group, and three sets of rwx permissions: owner, group, everyone else. chmod changes them (chmod 600 = only the owner can read and write), chgrp changes the group. Secrets should be readable by as few people as possible, and scripts need x to run.
explanation:
Run ls -l and the first column of each line looks like -rw-r--r--. The first character is the type (- for a file, d for a folder). The other nine are three groups of three: what the owner can do, what members of the file's group can do, and what everyone else can do. r is read, w is write, x is execute (for a folder, x means you can enter it). The next two columns name the owner and the group.

chmod changes permissions. The letter form is readable: chmod u+x deploy.sh adds execute for the user who owns it, chmod o-w removes write for others, chmod g+w adds write for the group. The number form sets all nine at once, one digit per group, adding read = 4, write = 2, execute = 1. So 644 is rw-r--r-- (the usual for files), 755 is rwxr-xr-x (scripts and folders), and 600 is rw------- (private: SSH keys, passwords, .env files).

Groups are how teams share. id shows which groups you belong to; chgrp devs folder hands a folder to the devs group, and then group permissions decide what the team can do with it. Only the owner (or root, the administrator) can change a file's permissions. On real servers you'll meet sudo, which runs a single command as root -- it's powerful precisely because it skips all of these checks, so use it only when you mean it.

Why it matters: a web server that can write to its own code can be made to rewrite it, and an API key in a world-readable file is readable by every process on the machine. Least privilege starts here.
